title: The Medium Is Not The Message
author: Noble, Andrew
summary: Andrew Noble pushes back on the popular misreading of Marshall McLuhan's famous phrase. McLuhan's actual claim was that every medium introduces new scales and consequences to human affairs—not that the medium erases or overrides the original content of communication. Noble agrees that media shape us and that technology has real personal and social consequences, but argues the popular reading goes too far: an 'I love you' sent by text differs in medium-effect from one spoken aloud, but the underlying content remains meaningfully distinct from the medium carrying it.
points: McLuhan's 'the medium is the message' is a rhetorical phrase designed to catch readers off-guard, not a literal claim that content is irrelevant—his actual argument is that technology has personal and social consequences.
Every medium is, for McLuhan, an extension of ourselves: a shovel extends the hand, a car the legs, a speaker the voice—and each extension changes the scale of human affairs.
McLuhan discusses over a dozen technologies—clothing, housing, clocks, print, comics—all carrying both a medium-effect and content that remains meaningfully distinct.
The popular reading implies that form completely overwrites content; Noble argues the medium is one message among others, not the only message.
The early church's shift from scroll to codex is an example where a medium change had real cultural consequences without fundamentally altering the content of the message carried.
quotes: In Marshall McLuhan’s book, The Extensions of Man, he describes what he means when he says his famous refrain, “the medium is the message.” He explains: This is merely to say that the personal and social consequences of any medium — that is, of any extension of ourselves — result from the new scale that is introduced into our affairs by each extension of ourselves, or by any new technology.

I hate to be so nitpicky about this, but it really can be confusing when you have a phrase like “the medium is the message” that people so readily wave their hand towards and assume we all know what it means.
Or if by saying it you mean, “the medium is the message that we should pay more attention to,” but not if you mean, “the medium is the only message.” Many people are welcome to speak in such ways.
And so, in my laws of technology, I say that “technology changes you.” This states one of the underlying points made by McLuhan more clearly: there are personal consequences to every technology.
There is some irony in the fact that all Substack posts on the internet must (by common thought) have an image to go with them, not to mention the fact that I used AI to make it.
The early church, for example, changed the Scriptures from being written on a scroll to being written in a codex (a precursor to the modern book, with pages).
